title: 道德經 第二十章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 20, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 62. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 20 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 異俗 (Unlike the Common Run). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
絕學無憂，
唯之與阿，
相去幾何？
善之與惡，
相去若何？
人之所畏，
不可不畏。

morph.gloss: to cut off, have done with
learning — book-study, the taking on of doctrine
the respectful 'yes' — the assent given to a superior (read wěi here, not wéi 'only')
particle: neither 'of' nor 'them' here — it merely holds the two things being set against each other
the offhand 'yeah' — a careless grunt of agreement
to stand apart, to be distant
how many, how much (read jǐ; jī is 'to verge on')
ugly, foul — è, the opposite of 善; not wù 'to loathe'
here the ordinary subject-marker before 所: 'what men fear'
that which — makes a noun of the verb after it
to fear, to stand in dread of
to fear — 不可不 is a double negative, 'cannot not'; who does the fearing is left unstated, as Chinese leaves it

sentences.l:
Cut off learning, and there is no worry.
'Yes, sir' as against 'yeah' —
how far apart?
Fine as against foul —
how far apart?
What men fear —
one cannot but fear.
sentences.i: Have done with learning and worry is at an end. A deferential 'yes' and a careless 'yeah' — how far apart are they? What is fine and what is foul — how far apart are they? Yet what men fear, one cannot help fearing.
sentences.n: 唯 and 阿 are two ways of saying yes: one respectful, one offhand. Nothing separates them but manners, and the question is whether 善 and 惡 are separated by any more. Note what 之 is doing — a third job for a character you have met as 'of' and as 'them': in 唯之與阿 it simply holds a pair together for comparison and is not translated. Then in 人之所畏 it does a fourth: it sits between a subject and its verb to turn the whole clause into a noun, 'what men fear'. The two questions also use different interrogatives, 幾何 'how much?' and 若何 'like what?', and come to the same thing. Two honest uncertainties. First, the chapter division: many editors join 絕學無憂 to the end of chapter 19, where it makes a fourth command of the same shape as the three there; the 81 chapters are traditional and carry no authority, so nothing rules on it. Second, the last line. 不可不畏 can be the speaker conceding that he too must fear what everyone fears, or it can be dry mockery of the concession. The Chinese decides neither, and there is nothing in the line to settle it. Manuscript note: where we read 阿, the Mawangdui silk manuscripts write 訶 hē, 'to scold' — assent against rebuke rather than polite against rude.

morph.gloss: waste, wild — untilled ground running out to no edge
the verse particle: a breath and a lift, with nothing to translate
to come to an end; the middle, the finishing point

sentences.l: Wild! — and it has not yet come to an end!
sentences.i: How boundless it is, and no end to it yet!
sentences.n: 兮 you met all through chapter 15; it will punctuate this chapter too. 未央, 'not yet at an end', was famous enough to be the name of the Han emperors' palace, the Weiyang Gong. What 'it' is, the text does not say — Chinese leaves the subject out and lets you supply it. The crowd's revelry, the distance between the speaker and them, the Way itself: all three have been read here. Wang Bi takes the sigh to measure how far the speaker stands from common custom.

sentences.t:
眾人熙熙，
如享太牢，
如春登臺。

morph.gloss: the multitude, the common run of people — everybody else
beaming and merry — a doubled word for a crowd all lit up with pleasure
to partake of an offering — to eat what has been set before the spirits
the Great Offering — ox, sheep and pig together, the fullest sacrifice there is, and the feast that follows it
the pen for sacrificial beasts; hence the beasts offered
a terrace — a raised platform built to stand on and look out from

sentences.l:
The crowd, beaming and merry,
as if partaking of the Great Offering,
as if climbing a terrace in spring.
sentences.i: The crowd are all merriment — as though feasting at the great sacrifice, as though climbing a terrace in spring.
sentences.n: 熙熙 is a doubled word, and this chapter runs on them: 儽儽, 沌沌, 昭昭, 昏昏, 察察, 悶悶 are all coming. Chinese doubles a word to paint a picture rather than to intensify it — you saw the device in chapter 6's 緜緜, thread drawn out without a break. From here on they get only a nudge. 太牢 was a ruler's sacrifice and nobody else's; the point of the line is that the crowd carry on as though every day were a state feast.

sentences.t:
我獨泊兮其未兆，
如嬰兒之未孩；

morph.gloss: alone — I and no one else
lying still, at anchor — unruffled, giving nothing away
it, he — pointing back at the speaker himself
to show a sign — properly the crack in a scorched tortoise-shell by which a diviner reads what is coming
a babe in arms, a newborn
a babe in arms, a newborn
subject-marker inside the clause: 'the infant's not yet having smiled'
to smile and gurgle as a baby does — a VERB here, not the modern noun 'child'

sentences.l:
I alone am still! — he has given no sign yet,
like an infant that has not yet smiled;
sentences.i: I alone lie quiet, giving no sign, like a newborn that has not yet smiled;
sentences.n: 兆 is a divination word: the cracks that run through a heated shell, which the diviner reads. To have not yet 兆-ed is to give nothing away in advance — no legible sign of what one will do. 孩 is a trap worth stopping at: in modern Chinese it is the noun 'child' (孩子), but classically it is the verb for an infant's first laugh, and that is the sense here. Reading a modern meaning back into an old character is the commonest quiet mistake in this language. 嬰兒 is one of the book's standing images — you met it in chapter 10 (能嬰兒乎, 'can you be an infant?') and it returns in chapter 28: the not-yet-shaped.

morph.gloss: worn out and drooping — a doubled word: slack, with nothing held up (a rare character; léi and lěi are both given for it)
to go home, to return where one belongs

sentences.l: Drooping and slack! — as if with nowhere to go home to.
sentences.n: Editions write this doubled word differently — 儽儽, 纍纍, 累累 all appear, and all point at the same thing hanging limp. 歸 is the word for going home: a bride going to her husband's house, a soul returning. Chapter 16 used it for the ten thousand things returning each to its root; this line is that line with the ground taken away.

sentences.t:
眾人皆有餘，
而我獨若遺。

morph.gloss: all of them (an adverb: it stands before the verb, not before the noun)
a surplus, more than is needed, what is left over
left behind, dropped and not picked up (read yí; wèi is 'to hand over')

sentences.l:
The crowd all have more than enough,
and yet I alone am as one left behind.
sentences.i: Everyone else has more than enough; I alone seem to have been left out.
sentences.n: 遺 is a thing dropped on the road and never claimed. 若 + a bare verb gives 'like one who has been ——ed', with no relative pronoun and no passive marker; position does all of it.

morph.gloss: a fool, a dullard — built exactly like 聖人 'the sage', and set against it
stupid, dull, slow to divide things up
the heart-mind — thinking and feeling in one organ
assertive final particle: closes the statement as settled

sentences.i: The heart of a dullard, that is what I have!
sentences.n: No verb at all: 我, then 'a fool's heart', then two particles. Chinese sets a topic down and comments on it, and English has to supply 'I have' or 'mine is'. 愚 is not plain insult here — the dullard's heart is the one that does not cut the world up into distinctions, which is precisely the 智 'cleverness' that chapter 19 has just told us to throw away. The two chapters are meant to be read together.

morph.gloss: muddled and unsorted — a doubled word: water churned until nothing in it can be told apart
turbid, confused; in 混沌, the primal chaos

sentences.n: 沌 is the character of 混沌, the undivided chaos before things were separated out — later the name of a faceless emperor in the Zhuangzi, who died when his friends drilled holes in him to give him a face. The speaker claims the word for his own mind, and means it as praise.

morph.gloss: worldly folk — people of the common custom
custom, the usual way of the world; vulgar, common
bright and glaring — a doubled word: lit up, everything on show

sentences.t:
我獨昏昏。
俗人察察，

morph.gloss: dim and dusky — a doubled word: the light gone out of it
keen and prying — a doubled word: examining, splitting hairs

sentences.l:
I alone am dim and dusky.
Worldly folk, keen and prying;
sentences.n: Two contrasts built out of doubled words, with no comparative and no 'whereas': 昭昭 against 昏昏 is bright against dim, and 察察 against the 悶悶 of the next line is sharp-eyed against shut-up. Setting the two clauses side by side is the whole construction. 昏 is the same character that darkened the state in chapter 18 (國家昏亂); here the speaker takes it for himself, and it is not a complaint.

sentences.t:
我獨悶悶。
澹兮其若海，

morph.gloss: shut up and unheeding — a doubled word: the lid on, nothing coming out
stopped up, stifled; dull, without spark
wide and level — the calm of open water
he — of himself again, in the third person

sentences.l:
I alone am shut up and dull.
Wide and calm! — he is as the sea,
sentences.i: I alone am muffled and dull. Placid as the open sea,
sentences.n: Notice the pronoun: 我 'I' in one line, 其 'he' in the next, both the speaker. Chinese slides between them without ceremony, and the shift is not a change of subject. Editions differ over how the first character here is written — 澹, 淡 and 憺 all appear, and all point at the same wide stillness.

morph.gloss: blowing high and free — of wind up aloft, where nothing checks it (a rare character; its reading is unsettled, liù and liáo are both given)
to stop, to come to rest

sentences.l: Blowing aloft! — as if never stopping.
sentences.i: Like wind high up, with nothing to bring it to a halt.
sentences.n: 飂 is rare enough that its pronunciation is not settled, and its exact sense is a guess from context and from the wind radical at the top. The line pairs with 澹兮其若海: the sea and the wind aloft, the two things with no edge to them. Compare 若無所歸 four units back: that one has 所, 'no place to return to', and this one has not — 無止 is simply 'no stopping', an act and not a place.

morph.gloss: a means, a wherewithal — the preposition 'by means of' standing here as a NOUN

sentences.l: The crowd all have their means;
sentences.i: Everyone else has something to go on;
sentences.n: 以 has been the workhorse preposition all through this book — 'by means of', 'so as to'. Here nothing follows it, and it is a noun: a wherewithal, a use to be put to, something to be getting on with. This is the fluidity of parts of speech at its sharpest: no ending changes, and the character does a different job because of where it stands.

morph.gloss: blockish, stubbornly unworked — of stone that will not take a shape
of the outer country — rustic, boorish, from the villages beyond the town

sentences.l: and yet I alone am blockish, like a boor.
sentences.i: and I alone am stubborn and unpolished, a bumpkin.
sentences.n: 鄙 is a place-word first: the outlying districts past the town wall, then the people who live there, then 'uncouth'. 頑 is stone that refuses to be carved, one chapter after we were told to hold on to the uncarved block. Both insults are claimed on purpose.

sentences.t:
我獨異於人，
而貴食母。

morph.gloss: from (the all-purpose preposition, standing after its verb)
to prize, to hold precious — the adjective 'costly' doing duty as a verb
that feeds, nourishing — read sì, the causative 'to give food to', not shí 'to eat'
mother — the source, as in chapter 1's 'mother of the ten thousand things'

sentences.l:
I alone differ from other men,
and prize the mother that feeds.
sentences.i: I alone am unlike other men: what I prize is the mother that feeds us.
sentences.n: 食母 is the chapter's crux, and the whole of it turns on how one character is read. Take 食 as shí 'to eat' and the line is 'I prize being fed by the mother'. Take it as sì — the causative, 'to give food to' — and 食母 is a phrase, the feeding mother, the nurse who suckles. Both are old readings; nothing in the manuscripts settles it. Wang Bi does not name a reading, but he treats 食母 as one thing and glosses it 生之本, 'the root that life comes from', which fits a nourisher rather than an act of eating — so that is the road we take, and this is where the choice was made. 母 reaches back to chapter 1, where what has a name is 'the mother of the ten thousand things' — and the chapter that began by throwing learning away ends by naming the one thing worth holding to.
